question: Persistent inflation, caused by the COVID-19 pandemic and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, has led to rising energy prices and higher living costs. More and more people are finding themselves under mounting pressure and are being hit harder by energy poverty. Moreover, the EU’s green transition could continue to drive up energy prices, which could in turn push the most vulnerable groups into poverty.
Although the data is incomplete, there is a variety of evidence which suggests that women are and will continue to be more affected by energy poverty than men1,2. 1.
Whilst EU legislation does indeed address the risk of energy poverty in general, why does it not explicitly envisage a gender-specific approach to the problem?

What is the Commission’s view on the accusation made by the Committee on Women’s Rights and Gender Equality that the Green Deal in its current form takes insufficient account of gender equality and risks exacerbating existing gender inequalities?
Does the Commission have any concrete proposals specifically to protect vulnerable groups from being driven into poverty as a result of the green transition?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.2.2024) The Commission proposed a holistic framework of measures to address the root causes of energy poverty and to ensure a just energy transition for all. Women, and in particular those who are single parents and older women, are particularly affected due to structural inequalities in income distribution, socioeconomic status, and the gender care gap.

As key European Green Deal instrument, Directive (EU) 2023/17911 introduces an EU wide definition of energy poverty, which supports Member States in identifying vulnerable people in energy poverty. Commission Recommendation 2023/2407 on energy poverty2 and its accompanying Staff Working Document SWD/2003/6473 provide a set of measures which Member States may implement.

The Recovery and Resilience Facility, the Social Investment and Skills Window of the InvestEU programme, the European Social Fund Plus and the European Regional Development Fund help to ensure access to housing and services.

From 2026, the Social Climate Fund will provide Member States with financial resources to address energy poverty through investments in energy efficiency, building renovations, clean heating and cooling, renewable energy and access to low and zero emission vehicles.
The vulnerability of women, especially single mothers, elderly women or women with disabilities, is recognised and the Social Climate Plans must demonstrate how they address it in relevant cases.

Regarding the integrated national energy and climate plans, the Commission Implementing Regulation 2022/22994 requires Member States to report on how the implementation of the planned measures contribute to the just transition. The promotion of both human rights and gender equality and approach to inequalities in energy poverty is assessed.
